content.text: Oil Prices Surge As Trump Orders Hormuz Blockade, Gas Costs 'Likely To Jump Again' Oil prices have surged again after President Donald Trump announced a naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz amid the US-Israeli war on Iran. A satellite image of the Strait of Hormuz and President Donald Trump. Photo Credit: Wikimedia Commons - NASA (left), The White House (right) 04/13/2026 10:22 a.m. West Texas Intermediate climbed to $103.60 per barrel and Brent crude rose to $102.07 as of 9 a.m. Monday, April 13. Both benchmarks were up about 7% since trading ended Friday, April 10.The spike followed a breakdown in US-Iran peace talks on Saturday, April 11. Negotiations in Islamabad ended without a deal, with US and Iranian officials split on Iran's nuclear program, control of the strait, war reparations, and frozen assets.Trump said the US would begin a blockade in the strait, where Iran has stopped traffic since the US and Israel launched their attacks at the end of February. "Effective immediately, the United States Navy, the Finest in the World, will begin the process of BLOCKADING any and all Ships trying to enter, or leave, the Strait of Hormuz," Trump posted on his social media platform Truth Social.US Central Command said it would start blocking all maritime traffic in and out of Iran's ports at 10 a.m. on April 13. Ships will be allowed to use the strait to reach non-Iranian ports. The Strait of Hormuz is a critical global oil corridor, responsible for 20% to 25% of global crude shipments. Before the war, roughly 20 million barrels of oil per day typically passed through the route connecting the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.The lack of a deal between the US, Israel, and Iran is expected to continue driving gasoline prices higher worldwide. "With a breakdown in talks and renewed escalation over the weekend, motorists should prepare for another round of price increases," said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. "The move toward a full blockade of the Strait of Hormuz is compounding global supply concerns and risks further disrupting flows, which pushed oil prices sharply higher in Sunday night trading. As a result, gasoline prices are likely to jump again this week, with diesel expected to follow, until there is a meaningful restoration of shipping through the strait." Here are the average gas prices across the Northeast and their weekly increases as of April 13, according to AAA:Connecticut - $4.09 (up $0.57)Maine - $4.04 (up $0.55)Maryland - $4.12 (up $0.59)Massachusetts - $3.97 (up $0.50)New Hampshire - $3.97 (up $0.51)New Jersey - $4.03 (up $0.50)New York - $4.13 (up $0.59)Pennsylvania - $4.15 (up $0.48)Rhode Island - $3.99 (up $0.53)Vermont - $4.10 (up $0.57)Virginia - $4.01 (up $0.60)Washington, DC - $4.28 (up $0.58)Industry experts say the prolonged war will continue to cause turmoil for global energy markets, CNBC reported."Investors are now back to the drawing board trying to reassess the fair value of stocks now that it's clear that there is no end in sight to the conflict in the Middle East," said Clark Bellin, president and chief investment officer at Bellwether Wealth. "The Strait of Hormuz is key for oil prices and overall market sentiment, and it's clear that there will be more saber-rattling over this waterway between the US and Iran this week." Many European nations have opposed Trump's actions in the strait.United Kingdom Prime Minister Keir Starmer said that Britain is "not supporting" the blockade, adding that he's focused on "bringing countries together to keep the straits open, not shut.""It is, in my view, vital that we get the strait open and fully open," Starmer told the BBC in a radio interview. Spanish defense minister Margarita Robles said that Trump's blockade plan "makes no sense," The New York Times reported."This is another episode in the downward spiral the world has been dragged into," she said.French President Emmanuel Macron posted on social media that France and the UK will work with dozens of countries on Hormuz-related disruptions "separate from the warring parties."
